domain:
    # Problem dimension
    N: size

    # Indices
    i: dim in [0, N)
    j: dim in [0, N)
    k: dim in [0, N)

data:
    # Working distance matrices (double-buffered), row-major:
    #   pathA[i, j]  <->  underlying storage offset = i * N + j
    #   pathB[i, j]  <->  underlying storage offset = i * N + j
    #
    # At the end of the computation, one of {pathA, pathB} contains the
    # all-pairs shortest-path distances (equivalent to "path" in the C code).
    pathA[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j
    pathB[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # Temporary buffer to hold the k-th row of the current path matrix,
    # so we don’t reload it N times from memory for every i:
    #   row_k[j] = path_cur[k, j]
    row_k[j]: temp DATA_TYPE = (j) -> j

parameters:
    INF: DATA_TYPE  # = (DATA_TYPE)999
    N:   int        # problem dimension
    # Tunable blocking and vectorization parameters
    TI:  int        # tile size along i (e.g., 32 or 64)
    TJ:  int        # tile size along j (e.g., 32 or 64)
    VEC: int        # vector width in elements (depends on DATA_TYPE and ISA)

computation:
    # -------------------------------
    # 1. Initialization (init_array)
    # -------------------------------
    # C original:
    #   path[i][j] = i*j%7+1;
    #   if ((i+j)%13 == 0 || (i+j)%7==0 || (i+j)%11 == 0)
    #      path[i][j] = 999;
    #
    # We initialize pathA, and leave pathB undefined (it will be written later).
    for i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
        base = ( (i * j) mod 7 ) + 1
        sum  = i + j
        cond = ((sum mod 13) == 0) or
               ((sum mod 7)  == 0) or
               ((sum mod 11) == 0)
        pathA[i, j] = if cond then INF else (DATA_TYPE)base

    # -----------------------------------------
    # 2. Floyd–Warshall dynamic programming
    # -----------------------------------------
    #
    # High-level mathematical semantics:
    #   For k from 0 to N-1:
    #     for all i, j:
    #       path_next[i, j] = min(path_cur[i, j],
    #                             path_cur[i, k] + path_cur[k, j])
    #   Then swap(path_cur, path_next)
    #
    # We implement this with double-buffering (pathA, pathB) and a
    # per-iteration row cache row_k[j] to avoid re-reading path_cur[k, j]
    # from memory for every i.
    #
    # At even k:  path_cur = pathA, path_next = pathB
    # At odd  k:  path_cur = pathB, path_next = pathA

    for k in seq(0, N):    # k is strictly sequential
        # Select which buffer is current and which is next
        if (k mod 2) == 0:
            # even k: read from pathA, write to pathB
            cur  = pathA
            next = pathB
        else:
            # odd k: read from pathB, write to pathA
            cur  = pathB
            next = pathA

        # 2.1 Preload the k-th row into a temporary buffer row_k
        #     This is done once per k, amortizing the cost of reading
        #     cur[k, j] across all i.
        for j in [0, N):
            row_k[j] = cur[k, j]

        # 2.2 Main DP update:
        #     next[i, j] = min(cur[i, j], cur[i, k] + cur[k, j])
        #                = min(cur[i, j], cur[i, k] + row_k[j])
        #
        # We tile i and j in the optimization section; here we express
        # the logical computation.
        for i in [0, N):
            # Load cur[i, k] once per i and reuse across all j.
            d_ik = cur[i, k]
            for j in [0, N):
                via_k   = d_ik + row_k[j]
                current = cur[i, j]
                next[i, j] = min(current, via_k)

    # After the loop, the final result resides in:
    #   if (N mod 2) == 0 then pathA else pathB

dependencies:
    # Initialization must complete before any DP iterations.
    for i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
        init_pathA(i, j) -> fw_update(k=0, i, j)

    # For each k, all updates for k depend on completion of k-1.
    # (cur, next buffers enforce this dataflow.)
    for k in [1, N), i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
        fw_update(k-1, i, j) -> fw_update(k, i, j)

optimization:
    # -----------------------------------------
    # Loop blocking (tiling) for cache locality
    # -----------------------------------------
    # We tile the i and j loops inside each k-iteration. Each tile
    # operates on a TI x TJ submatrix of 'cur' and 'next'. This improves
    # temporal locality and reduces cache misses for large N.
    #
    # Conceptually transforms:
    #   for i in [0, N):
    #     for j in [0, N):
    #       ...
    # into:
    #   for I in [0, N) step TI:
    #     for J in [0, N) step TJ:
    #       for i in [I, min(I+TI, N)):
    #         for j in [J, min(J+TJ, N)):
    #           ...
    block(i, I, TI)   # I: outer tile index for rows
    block(j, J, TJ)   # J: outer tile index for columns

    # Ensure the k-loop is outermost (global phase iteration),
    # then tile loops I and J inside k:
    hoist(k)
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)

    # -----------------------------------------
    # Parallelization
    # -----------------------------------------
    # For a fixed k, all (i, j) updates read from 'cur' and write to
    # disjoint entries of 'next', so they are independent and can be
    # parallelized.
    #
    # We parallelize over tiles (I, J), which gives coarser-grained
    # tasks and better cache behavior than parallelizing over raw i or j.
    # On a 32-core CPU, TI and TJ should be chosen so that the working set
    # per tile (2 * TI * TJ * sizeof(DATA_TYPE)) fits in the L2 cache.
    parallelize(I)
    # Optionally also parallelize J on very large N; beware of
    # over-subscription if both I and J are parallel.
    # parallelize(J)

    # -----------------------------------------
    # Vectorization
    # -----------------------------------------
    # Inside each tile, we vectorize across the innermost j-dimension
    # to exploit SIMD units. Choose VEC according to DATA_TYPE and ISA
    # (e.g., VEC=8 for float with AVX2, VEC=16 for float with AVX-512).
    vectorize(j, VEC)

    # -----------------------------------------
    # Scalar hoisting and reuse
    # -----------------------------------------
    # The scalar d_ik = cur[i, k] is invariant in the inner j-loop;
    # we explicitly hoist it to avoid redundant loads.
    #
    # (Already reflected in the computation section by introducing d_ik,
    # included here to emphasize that code generation should keep it
    # in a register across the j-loop.)
    hoist(d_ik)

    # -----------------------------------------
    # Row-k caching
    # -----------------------------------------
    # row_k[j] is computed once per k and reused for all i.
    # Its size is N, so the extra memory is O(N), which is far less
    # than the original 2*N^2 footprint (< 50% overhead even for small N).
    #
    # To keep row_k hot in cache, we can optionally tile its use in sync
    # with J:
    #   for each tile J:
    #     load row_k[J : J+TJ) into L1 (implicitly via normal loads)
    #     use it for all i in [I, I+TI)
    #
    # This is already implied by the 'block(j, J, TJ)' transformation,
    # but we document it here as an intended optimization.

    # -----------------------------------------
    # Unrolling
    # -----------------------------------------
    # If TJ and/or TI are small constants (e.g., 16 or 32), partial or
    # full unrolling of the inner loops can reduce loop overhead and
    # expose more ILP; keep factors modest to avoid code bloat.
    unroll(j, factor = min(TJ, VEC))  # unroll by up to VEC inside a tile

    # -----------------------------------------
    # Notes on memory footprint
    # -----------------------------------------
    # Original Floyd–Warshall code uses 2 * N^2 elements (path0, path1).
    # This optimized version still uses:
    #   pathA: N^2
    #   pathB: N^2
    #   row_k: N
    # Total = 2 * N^2 + N elements, which is well within the allowed
    # < 1.5x increase of the original memory footprint.

```text
domain:
    # Problem size
    n: dim in [0, N)

    # Matrix indices
    i: dim in [0, N)   # row index
    j: dim in [0, N)   # column index
    k: dim in [0, N)   # Floyd–Warshall iteration, must be sequential

data:
    # Double-buffered distance matrices (row-major: path[r][c] -> r * N + c)
    path_curr[i, j]: inout  DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j
    path_next[i, j]: scratch DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # 1D temporaries for current k-th row and column to reduce redundant loads
    row_k[i]: scratch DATA_TYPE = (i) -> i       # stores path_curr[i, k]
    col_k[j]: scratch DATA_TYPE = (j) -> j       # stores path_curr[k, j]

parameters:
    # Tuning parameters for cache/SIMD on the target machine
    T_I: int > 0  # tile size along i (rows), e.g. 32 or 64
    T_J: int > 0  # tile size along j (cols), e.g. 32 or 64
    T_K: int > 0  # tile size along k, e.g. 1–8 (still processed sequentially inside each tile)
    V:   int > 0  # vector width for innermost j-loop, e.g. 4 or 8

computation:
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Initialization (matches init_array): set initial path_curr[i,j].
    # C layout: path[i][j] is mapped to path_curr(i,j) with row-major layout.
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    for i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
        base = ((i * j) % 7) + 1   # integer arithmetic
        sum  = i + j
        if ( (sum % 13 == 0) or (sum % 7 == 0) or (sum % 11 == 0) ):
            path_curr[i, j] = cast(DATA_TYPE, 999)
        else:
            path_curr[i, j] = cast(DATA_TYPE, base)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Floyd–Warshall dynamic programming with double buffering.
    #
    # For each k we compute:
    #   path_next[i,j] = min( path_curr[i,j],
    #                         path_curr[i,k] + path_curr[k,j] )
    # then swap roles of (path_curr, path_next).
    #
    # Using separate buffers per k-iteration guarantees that all reads
    # of path_curr[*,k] and path_curr[k,*] see the same "previous" matrix,
    # which matches the Halide code’s semantics.
    #
    # Additionally, we precompute the k-th row and column into 1D buffers
    # row_k and col_k to avoid reloading path_curr[i,k] and path_curr[k,j]
    # N times each for every (i,j) pair.
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    for k in seq[0, N):        # k must advance sequentially
        # Precompute row_k[i] = path_curr[i, k] for all i.
        for i in [0, N):
            row_k[i] = path_curr[i, k]

        # Precompute col_k[j] = path_curr[k, j] for all j.
        for j in [0, N):
            col_k[j] = path_curr[k, j]

        # Main Floyd–Warshall update for this k, writing into path_next.
        for i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
            via_k = row_k[i] + col_k[j]
            path_next[i, j] = min(path_curr[i, j], via_k)

        # Swap buffers logically: next becomes current for the next k.
        # Semantically this is equivalent to copying, but will be
        # implemented as a constant-time pointer swap (see optimization).
        for i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
            path_curr[i, j] = path_next[i, j]

optimization:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Keep row-major traversal with j as the fast-varying dimension.
    #
    #    All 2D loops over (i,j) are structured so that:
    #      - i is the outer loop
    #      - j is the inner loop
    #    This matches the memory layout path[i][j] -> i * N + j,
    #    giving unit-stride access for j.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    interchange(i, j)    # ensure j is innermost wherever beneficial

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Tile the (i,j) space to improve cache locality.
    #
    #    For the main Floyd–Warshall update, we apply 2D blocking:
    #      - I is the tile index along i, J along j.
    #      - Within each tile we still iterate with j innermost.
    #
    #    This keeps small blocks of path_curr and path_next in cache
    #    while updating them for a fixed k, and reduces cache thrashing
    #    when N is large.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    block(i, I, T_I)     # i  -> I (outer tile), i (inner in-tile index)
    block(j, J, T_J)     # j  -> J (outer tile), j (inner in-tile index)
    hoist(I)             # outermost: iterate tiles in I first
    hoist(J)             # then tiles in J

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. (Optional) Tile the k dimension for better reuse of row_k/col_k.
    #
    #    We can process k in blocks of size T_K:
    #      for K in [0, N) step T_K:
    #        for k in [K, min(K+T_K, N)):
    #          ...
    #
    #    This is still semantically equivalent because k remains the
    #    outermost sequential loop, but gives the compiler an explicit
    #    structure that can help instruction cache and branch prediction
    #    when T_K is small.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    block(k, K, T_K)
    hoist(K)             # K loop outermost, k inside it, still sequential

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Parallelization.
    #
    #    For a fixed k, all (i,j) updates are independent: each writes
    #    to a distinct path_next[i,j] and only reads from path_curr[*][*]
    #    and from row_k, col_k (which are read-only in this phase).
    #
    #    Thus, for each (K, k) we can:
    #      - parallelize across tiles in I (row blocks), and/or
    #      - parallelize across tiles in J (column blocks).
    #
    #    We must *not* parallelize across k or K due to DP dependencies.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    parallelize(I)       # distribute tiles of rows across threads
    # parallelize(J)     # optionally also distribute across columns if
                         # N is large and core count is high

    # Precomputation loops for row_k and col_k are O(N), so their
    # cost is small; we leave them sequential or lightly parallelized
    # (e.g., across i or j) if profiling indicates a benefit.

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Vectorization.
    #
    #    Vectorize the innermost j-loop inside each (i, k) tile.
    #    Since j is unit-stride in memory, this maps naturally to
    #    SIMD loads/stores of path_curr[i,j], path_next[i,j], and
    #    col_k[j].
    #
    #    V should be chosen to match the hardware SIMD width,
    #    e.g. V=8 for AVX2 + float, V=4 for AVX2 + double, etc.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    vectorize(j, V)      # innermost dimension in the main update
    vectorize(j, V)      # also apply to col_k precompute
    vectorize(i, V)      # apply to row_k precompute if beneficial

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 6. Double-buffer swap optimization.
    #
    #    The explicit copy:
    #      for i, j: path_curr[i,j] = path_next[i,j]
    #
    #    is semantically a logical swap of the two matrices.
    #    We replace this O(N^2) copy with a constant-time pointer swap:
    #
    #      swap_buffers(path_curr, path_next)
    #
    #    # swap_buffers(A, B) indicates that after the loop over k,
    #    # the roles of A and B as "current" and "next" matrices are
    #    # exchanged by swapping references, without data movement.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # swap_buffers is a conceptual optimization that preserves semantics.
    swap_buffers(path_curr, path_next)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 7. Unrolling small inner loops (optional).
    #
    #    For small tile sizes T_J, partial unrolling of the innermost
    #    j-loop can reduce loop overhead and improve ILP:
    #
    #      unroll(j, U)   with U a small factor of T_J, e.g. U=2 or U=4.
    #
    #    This should be chosen empirically, as too much unrolling may
    #    cause I-cache pressure.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # unroll(j, 2)
```

domain:
    # N: global problem size (number of vertices)
    i: dim in [0, N)          # row index (C: first index of path[i][j])
    j: dim in [0, N)          # column index (C: second index of path[i][j])
    k: dim in [0, N)          # Floyd–Warshall intermediate vertex

data:
    # Single logical distance matrix, as in the original C code.
    # Row-major layout: path[i][j] lives at offset i * N + j.
    path[i, j]: inout num_t = (i, j) -> i * N + j  # C path[i][j]

parameters:
    N: int           # matrix order
    INF: num_t       # large sentinel value for "no edge" (e.g., 999)

computation:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Initialization: identical to init_array() / original C loop.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    init_path:
        for i, j:
            base = (i * j % 7) + 1
            if ((i + j) % 13 == 0) or ((i + j) % 7 == 0) or ((i + j) % 11 == 0):
                path[i, j] = INF
            else:
                path[i, j] = base

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Floyd–Warshall dynamic program:
    #
    # for (k = 0; k < N; k++)
    #   for (i = 0; i < N; i++)
    #     for (j = 0; j < N; j++)
    #       path[i][j] = min(path[i][j], path[i][k] + path[k][j]);
    #
    # We keep k sequential and exploit parallelism + locality in (i, j).
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    floyd_warshall:
        for k in seq(0, N):         # k must be sequential because step k+1 depends on step k
            for i in [0, N):
                # Local scalar reused across all j for fixed (k, i).
                # This avoids reloading path[i, k] inside the j-loop.
                a_ik = path[i, k]
                for j in [0, N):
                    path[i, j] = min(path[i, j], a_ik + path[k, j])

dependencies:
    # Initialization must complete before the DP starts.
    for i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
        init_path(i, j) -> floyd_warshall(k, i, j)

optimization:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Cache-friendly tiling of (i, j)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # TI, TJ, TK, VEC, UNR are tunable constants (e.g., via build-time knobs):
    #   TI: tile size in i (rows), typically 32–128 (L1/L2 sized)
    #   TJ: tile size in j (cols), typically 32–128
    #   TK: k-block size, typically small (1–8) or left as 1
    #   VEC: vector width in elements (e.g., 8 for AVX2 float, 4–8 for num_t)
    #   UNR: small unroll factor for the innermost loop (e.g., 2 or 4)
    #
    # We tile i and j inside each k-iteration to improve temporal locality
    # for path[k, j] and for rows of path[i, j].
    block(i, I, TI)                 # tile rows: I enumerates row-tiles, i enumerates rows inside a tile
    block(j, J, TJ)                 # tile columns: J enumerates col-tiles, j enumerates cols inside a tile

    # Effective loop structure:
    #   for k in seq(0, N):
    #     for I:
    #       for J:
    #         for i in I:
    #           a_ik = path[i, k]       # one strided read per (k, i)
    #           for j in J:
    #             path[i, j] = min(path[i, j], a_ik + path[k, j])

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Parallelism across tiles
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # For a fixed k, all (i, j) updates are independent (they write
    # distinct elements of path), so we can parallelize over tiles.
    parallelize(I)                  # distribute row-tiles I across CPU threads
    # (Optionally also parallelize over J for very large N and many cores:
    #  parallelize(J), ensuring not to oversubscribe threads.)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Vectorization and unrolling
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # j is the fastest-varying dimension in memory, so vectorizing j gives
    # unit-stride loads/stores for both path[i, j] and path[k, j].
    vectorize(j, VEC)               # SIMD over columns inside each tile
    unroll(j, UNR)                  # small unroll of the (possibly vectorized) inner loop

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. k-blocking (optional, remains sequential)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # k-blocking groups several consecutive k-iterations so that a working
    # set of tiles can stay hot in cache; semantics are preserved because
    # the inner k still runs in increasing order.
    # High-level structure:
    #   for K in seq(0, N) step TK:
    #     for k in [K, min(K+TK, N)):
    #       ... tiled/parallelized (i,j) loop as above ...
    block(k, K, TK)                 # K outer (sequential), k inner (sequential inside each block)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Scalar hoisting (already reflected in computation)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # We have already hoisted path[i, k] into a_ik outside the j-loop in
    # the computation section. This reduces:
    #   - loads of path[i, k] from O(N^3) to O(N^2)
    #   - address arithmetic for that access.
    #
    # A similar (optional) micro-optimization is to prefetch or cache a
    # tile of the k-th row path[k, j] per (k, J) tile, using a temporary
    # 1D buffer of length TJ; this adds O(N * TJ) extra storage, which is
    # negligible (< 1% of path’s N^2 elements) and well within the
    # allowed memory overhead.

```text
domain:
    i: dim in [0, N)          # row index
    j: dim in [0, N)          # column index
    k: dim in [0, N)          # Floyd–Warshall intermediate vertex

data:
    # Main distance matrix: C-style path[i][j], stored row-major.
    path[i, j]: inout num_t = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # Temporary matrix for ping‑pong (double buffering) implementation.
    path_tmp[i, j]: tmp num_t = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # Optional per‑k temporaries to cache the k‑th row and column.
    # They are length-N vectors and are negligible vs N×N.
    row_k[j]: tmp num_t = j        # conceptually row_k[j] = path[k, j]
    col_k[i]: tmp num_t = i        # conceptually col_k[i] = path[i, k]

parameters:
    N: int
    INF: num_t = (num_t)999        # sentinel distance used in initialization

computation:
    # Initialization (matches init_array):
    #   path[i][j] = i*j%7+1
    #   if ((i+j)%13 == 0 || (i+j)%7 == 0 || (i+j)%11 == 0) path[i][j] = 999;
    for i, j:
        base = ((i * j) % 7) + 1
        if ((i + j) % 13 == 0) or ((i + j) % 7 == 0) or ((i + j) % 11 == 0):
            path[i, j] = INF
        else:
            path[i, j] = (num_t)base

    # Floyd–Warshall dynamic programming:
    # Standard semantics: for each k, relax all pairs (i, j) via vertex k.
    # This is the all‑pairs shortest path over an adjacency matrix.
    for k in seq([0, N)):
        for i, j:
            path[i, j] = min(path[i, j],
                              path[i, k] + path[k, j])

optimization:
    # 1. Memory layout and loop order
    # path[i, j] is row‑major, so j should be the innermost loop to get
    # contiguous accesses for path[i, j] and path[k, j].
    interchange(j, i)

    # 2. Double buffering to remove intra‑iteration dependencies
    # The recurrence conceptually reads path^k and writes path^{k+1}. To avoid
    # read‑after‑write hazards within a k‑iteration and enable aggressive
    # parallelization, implement the update using explicit ping‑pong buffers:
    #
    #   for k in seq([0, N)):
    #       for i, j:
    #           path_tmp[i, j] = min(path[i, j],
    #                                path[i, k] + path[k, j])
    #       swap(path, path_tmp)
    #
    # This preserves the mathematical Floyd–Warshall semantics but makes
    # every (i, j) update at fixed k independent, since all reads come from
    # path and all writes go to path_tmp.
    # (swap(path, path_tmp) is a conceptual pointer swap, not a data copy.)

    # 3. Cache tiling of the spatial domain (i, j)
    # Tile the i and j loops inside each k‑iteration to improve cache locality
    # and reduce working‑set size per core.
    #
    # TI, TJ are tunable tile sizes (e.g., TI = 32, TJ = 64) chosen such that
    # a TI×TJ tile of path plus frequently‑used rows/columns fits in L1/L2.
    block(i, I, TI)    # i = I * TI + i_in  (implicit inner i_in loop)
    block(j, J, TJ)    # j = J * TJ + j_in  (implicit inner j_in loop)

    # After tiling and loop interchange, the inner structure for fixed k is:
    #   for I:
    #     for J:
    #       for i_in:
    #         for j_in:
    #           ...

    # 4. Parallelism within each k‑iteration
    # Due to DP dependence, k must remain sequential (seq), but tiles in the
    # (i, j) plane for a given k are independent (because of double buffering).
    # Parallelize across outer i‑tiles; this provides coarse‑grained tasks.
    parallelize(I)

    # If N is large, you may also parallelize both I and J (2D tiling) as long
    # as each (I, J) tile writes a disjoint region of path_tmp. For simplicity
    # we parallelize only I here.

    # instruction‑level parallelism without blowing up register usage.
    # UI should divide TI and be small (e.g., 2 or 4).
    unroll(i, UI)
```

```text
domain:
    # Original C indices: path[i][j], with i,j ∈ [0, N)
    i: dim in [0, N)
    j: dim in [0, N)
    # Floyd–Warshall DP iteration index k
    k: dim in [0, N)

data:
    # Single logical distance matrix, row-major as in C: path[i][j]
    # (Halide’s Buffer(j,i) mapping is an implementation detail and is
    # abstracted away here.)
    path[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j  # row-major

    # Optional scratch buffer for implementations that want to use
    # double-buffering or blocked updates. Size is N×N, i.e. +100% over
    # a single matrix; the original Halide code already uses two buffers,
    # so this does not exceed its memory footprint.
    path_tmp[i, j]: scratch DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

parameters:
    N: int                         # problem size
    INF: DATA_TYPE                 # sentinel for "no edge", = 999
    # Tunable blocking and vectorization parameters (chosen offline
    # for the target machine, e.g. 32-core x64 with large LLC).
    TI: int                        # tile size for i (e.g. 64)
    TJ: int                        # tile size for j (e.g. 64)
    VEC_J: int                     # vector width for j (e.g. 8 or 16)
    PAR_I: int                     # number of parallel i-tiles (≤ number of cores)

computation:
    # 1. Initialization: path[i][j] = i*j%7+1, then possibly 999.
    init_base:
        for i, j:
            path[i, j] = (i * j % 7) + 1

    init_mask:
        for i, j:
            if ((i + j) % 13 == 0) or ((i + j) % 7 == 0) or ((i + j) % 11 == 0):
                path[i, j] = INF

    # 2. Floyd–Warshall dynamic programming:
    #
    # For each intermediate vertex k (sequentially),
    # update all pairs (i, j):
    #
    #     path[i][j] = min(path[i][j], path[i][k] + path[k][j])
    #
    # Semantically this matches the Halide floyd_step Func, which
    # is executed once per k over the whole matrix, double-buffered
    # at the implementation level.
    dp:
        for k in seq([0, N)):
            for i, j:
                path[i, j] = min(path[i, j], path[i, k] + path[k, j])

optimization:
    # Keep the DP dimension k as the outermost sequential loop.
    # This preserves the dependence chain across k-iterations.
    hoist(k)          # ensure k is outermost
    # (Implicitly: do not parallelize k.)

    # Block the (i, j) iteration space for better cache locality.
    # We tile rows and columns into TI×TJ blocks. This does not
    # change semantics because all (i, j) updates for a fixed k
    # are independent of each other.
    #
    # for k:
    #   for I in [0, ceil(N/TI)):
    #     for J in [0, ceil(N/TJ)):
    #       for i in [I*TI, min((I+1)*TI, N)):
    #         for j in [J*TJ, min((J+1)*TJ, N)):
    #           ...
    block(i, I, TI)
    block(j, J, TJ)

    # Parallelize across i-tiles (I). For a fixed k, each tile
    # (I, J) updates a disjoint region path[i,j], and the only
    # values read are from the same k-slice (path[*][k], path[k][*]).
    # Thus there are no cross-tile write–write or write–read hazards,
    # and tiles can execute in parallel.
    parallelize(I)

    # Within each tile, iterate j as the innermost dimension so that
    # path[i, j] and path[k, j] are accessed in contiguous memory
    # (row-major). This matches the original Halide reorder(j, i).
    hoist(J)          # J outside the inner i,j loops
    # Implicit nesting for each k:
    #   for I:
    #     for J:
    #       for i in tile I:
    #         for j in tile J:  # innermost

    # Vectorize along the innermost j-dimension. For each fixed
    # (k, i, I, J), the updates:
    #
    #   path[i, j..j+VEC_J-1] =

    #           path[i, k] + path[k, j..j+VEC_J-1])
    #
    # can be carried out with SIMD instructions. This preserves
    # semantics because each lane computes an independent (i, j).
    vectorize(j, VEC_J)

    # Optional: hoist the access path[i, k] out of the j-loop
    # within each (k, i) to reduce redundant loads. In imperative
    # code this would correspond to:
    #
    #   for k:

    #             path[i, j] = min(path[i, j], pik + path[k, j])
    #
    # which does not change the mathematical result.
    # We model this as a loop-invariant hoisting over j.
    hoist(j)          # with respect to the scalar expression path[i, k]
```
